I will keep my land in the crop pattern that fits Quzhou best: winter wheat first, then summer maize on the same fields. I’m making that choice because Quzhou is a typical North China Plain wheat-maize rotation area, with most cropland in that system, and the local “green ton-and-a-half grain” work in the county has been built around exactly that route. I’m also looking at the season: on April 16, 2026, my winter wheat is already in the ground and entering spring management, so I will finish this wheat crop well and then turn the land quickly into summer maize. I am assuming I am managing 10 mu of irrigated land, and I will keep all 10 mu in one annual rotation instead of splitting it into cash crops, because grain is what matches the local land, water, machinery, and my need for a steady, lower-risk year.

I will not chase the highest demonstration-field yield, but I will follow the same direction: improved seed for wheat, hybrid seed for maize, moderate nitrogen, steady phosphorus and potassium, and controlled irrigation. For wheat I will plough ahead of the season and hold to three irrigations because wheat in Quzhou depends more on irrigation. For maize I will switch fast after wheat harvest and use no-tillage on the wheat stubble so I do not lose time or soil moisture. I will keep pesticide sprays limited but timely, mainly to hold disease and insects in check rather than spray too often. My target yields are below the 2024 county demonstration fields, but still solid and realistic for a careful working year. Sources I used for this decision: [China Agricultural University Quzhou station on Quzhou’s wheat-maize technology](https://qzsyz.cau.edu.cn/art/2024/2/25/art_46232_1012984.html), [Quzhou 2024 demo yields and nitrogen/irrigation figures](https://qzsyz.cau.edu.cn/art/2024/10/8/art_46317_1039835.html), and [Quzhou wheat seedling survey showing the county’s wheat base](https://qzsyz.cau.edu.cn/art/2024/2/22/art_46317_1012731.html).
